extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners working on federated learning, distributed ML, privacy, and systems
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance, standards, evaluation dimensions, and practical constraints for researching, implementing, simulating, and reporting work in federated learning (cross-device and cross-silo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Federated Learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Federated learning is a machine learning setting where multiple entities (clients) collaborate in solving a machine learning problem, under the coordination of a central server or service provider. Each client’s raw data is stored locally and not exchanged or transferred; instead, focused updates intended for immediate aggregation are used to achieve the learning objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focused updates are updates narrowly scoped to contain the minimum information necessary for the specific learning task at hand; aggregation is performed as early as possible in the service of data minimization. This definition distinguishes FL from fully decentralized (peer-to-peer) learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify the FL setting precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting FL research, precisely describe the details of the particular FL setting of interest, particularly when the proposed approach makes assumptions that may not be appropriate in all settings (e.g. stateful clients that participate in all rounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because FL can encompass many problems, be explicit about cross-device vs cross-silo assumptions, client availability, data partitioning, addressability, reliability, and other deployment constraints so readers can judge applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducible simulation details
rubrics_metrics.description: Details of any simulations should be presented in order to make research reproducible; explain which aspects of the real-world setting the simulation is designed to capture (and which it is not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include dataset partitioning, client sampling, drop-out models, communication modeling, and any instrumentation that mimics deployment behavior. State limitations of the simulation and what real-world behaviors are omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about computation and communication locations
rubrics_metrics.description: For any proposed approach it is important to be unambiguous about where computation happens as well as what is communicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privacy and communication efficiency are first-order concerns in FL; specify whether computation occurs on-device, on-server, or in secure computation primitives, and list exact messages, bytes, and aggregates exchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lifecycle stages for FL model development
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical lifecycle: (1) Problem identification; (2) Client instrumentation; (3) Simulation prototyping (optional); (4) Federated model training; (5) (Federated) model evaluation; (6) Deployment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or building an FL system, ensure each lifecycle stage is addressed (e.g., instrumentation respects data minimization; evaluations include federated evaluation or held-out client testing; deployment uses staged rollouts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical federated training process steps
rubrics_metrics.description: A server repeats: (1) Client selection; (2) Broadcast of model weights and training program; (3) Client computation (local updates); (4) Aggregation of device updates; (5) Model update on server.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each step brings constraints and evaluation criteria: client eligibility (e.g. power/wifi), straggler handling, secure aggregation, compression, DP mechanisms, and update clipping. Be explicit about selection and dropout policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of client computation, aggregation, and model update
rubrics_metrics.description: Design choice to separate client computation, aggregation, and model update to enable composition of techniques like compression, differential privacy, and MPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This separation is not required (e.g. asynchronous SGD), but facilitates modular research: develop aggregation primitives (sums/means) and compose them with optimization algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid impacting user experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Training must not slow devices or degrade user experience; models used during training should be ephemeral and not shown to users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure client selection (idle, plugged-in, on unmetered Wi‑Fi) and constrain training to times that won't affect users; use staged rollout for deployment so flawed models don't reach broad population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish cross-device vs cross-silo FL
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-device: massive numbers of mobile/IoT devices, highly unreliable, typically stateless participants, fixed example-partitioned data, limited bandwidth. Cross-silo: small number of reliable organizations (2–100), stateful participation, potentially feature-partitioned data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose evaluation metrics and algorithmic assumptions that match the chosen variant; many techniques applicable to one may not apply to the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core characteristic: Data availability and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: FL settings can have decentralized, unbalanced, and non-IID data; clients' data is generated locally and cannot be re-shuffled centrally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments and algorithms that explicitly account for non-IID distributions and unbalanced per-client sample counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core characteristic: Scale and client counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Scale varies: datacenter distributed learning (clients = cluster nodes), cross-silo (1–100), cross-device (up to 10^10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report and evaluate with realistic client counts or appropriate simulations; small-scale experiments may not generalize to cross-device scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core characteristic: Primary bottleneck (computation vs communication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Datacenter training: computation bottleneck; cross-device FL: communication is often primary bottleneck (e.g., slow Wi‑Fi), though cross-silo may be either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure bytes uploaded/downloaded, number of communication rounds, and per-round latency; optimize accordingly depending on the bottleneck.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core characteristic: Orchestration and topology
rubrics_metrics.description: Federated learning typically uses central orchestration (hub-and-spoke), while fully decentralized learning uses peer-to-peer topologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State orchestration model (central server vs decentralized) and evaluate algorithms under that topology including message routing, node degrees, and link reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core characteristic: Addressability and client identity
rubrics_metrics.description: In some FL settings clients can be indexed (addressable); in large cross-device settings clients may not be indexable and participation is by sampling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether client identifiers are used for personalization, statefulness, or auditing; inclusion/exclusion policies affect privacy and bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core characteristic: Client statefulness and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Clients may be stateful (participate across rounds) or stateless (participate rarely); cross-device clients are often stateless and highly unreliable (dropout rates expected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithm design and evaluation must handle dropouts, partially completed work, and variable participation patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data partition axis (horizontal vs vertical/feature-partitioned)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data can be example-partitioned (horizontal) or feature-partitioned (vertical); FL methods and privacy concerns differ across partitioning axes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying cross-silo settings, consider vertical FL techniques and datasets; specify partitioning strategy used in experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting realistic order-of-magnitude operational metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Report typical sizes: total population size, devices selected per round, total devices that participate, number of rounds for convergence, wall-clock training time (e.g. Table 2: 10^6–10^10 devices, 50–5000 per round, 10^5–10^7 total participants, 500–10000 rounds, 1–10 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these operational metrics to contextualize experiments and to enable comparisons across works; report bytes transferred, rounds, and wall-clock time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulation fidelity and dataset partitioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Simulations should capture partitioned datasets, client variability, time-varying client arrival, and dropout correlated with local data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the partitioning strategy, retain metadata (timestamps, geolocation), and justify how the simulated clients map to the intended FL deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate benchmark datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend benchmarking on federated datasets like EMNIST (3,400 unbalanced clients), StackOverflow (342,477 users), Shakespeare (715 characters), and other cross-silo datasets (iNaturalist, Google-Landmark-v2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose datasets whose scale and non-IID characteristics reflect the target application; for scale-sensitive questions prefer StackOverflow or suitably partitioned large datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for feature-partitioned datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a need for more feature-partitioned (vertical) datasets to study cross-silo FL where different institutions hold disjoint feature sets for the same samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying vertical FL, use or create datasets partitioned by features and document the partitioning rationale (e.g., medical records split across institutes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Software/framework selection for simulation vs production
rubrics_metrics.description: Use simulation-oriented frameworks (TensorFlow Federated, FedML, PySyft, Leaf) for research prototyping and production-oriented frameworks (FATE, PaddleFL, Clara, IBM Federated Learning, Flower, Fedlearner) when addressing deployment concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the platform used and its limitations (e.g., simulation vs real-device constraints). For production work, evaluate authentication, communication protocols, encryption, and deployment mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication and compression evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess communication efficiency via metrics like bytes uploaded/downloaded, compression loss, and effects on convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing compression or quantization, measure impact on model quality, convergence rounds, wall-clock time, and downstream privacy/robustness interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy guarantees and where privacy fits in evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Privacy (e.g., differential privacy, secure aggregation, MPC) is a first-order concern; be explicit about privacy threat models, actors, and which protections are in place (central DP, distributed DP, secure computation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report formal privacy parameters (ε, δ) where applicable, and analyze tradeoffs between privacy, utility, communication, and robustness. Explain what is revealed to each actor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness to adversaries and failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate defenses and failure modes: model update poisoning, data poisoning, Byzantine clients, non-malicious dropouts, and tensions between privacy and robustness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include threat models, attacker capabilities, and empirical testing against attacks; report detection/mitigation effectiveness and residual vulnerabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and bias evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess sources of bias (in training data, system-induced), fairness without access to sensitive attributes, and interactions between fairness, privacy, and robustness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify per-group performance, analyze system-induced biases (e.g., device availability profiles), and evaluate methods that leverage federation to improve model diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: System and deployment constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for platform development, on-device runtime requirements, system parameter tuning, and device availability profiles when evaluating FL systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure latency, energy, memory, scheduling constraints, and deployment complexity; document assumptions about device state and orchestration mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of decentralized / peer-to-peer variants
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering fully decentralized learning, evaluate effects of network topology, asynchrony, message drops, local-update schedules, consensus speed, and spectral gap on convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report topology properties, synchronization model, frequency of local updates before communication, and how these choices affect wall-clock time and convergence under non-IID data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain which real-world behaviors are captured by proposed benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: For any benchmark or simulation, explicitly explain which real-world behaviors are modeled (e.g., diurnal availability patterns, client heterogeneity) and which are omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps readers assess external validity — success on a simulated benchmark should be tied to specific modeled constraints; otherwise state limitations.
